SpacerMap's Download numbered file now contains Spacer_ID / Spacer_Sequence pairs, without array membership; it cannot reconstruct the arrays. Use the array-map SVG or copy the normalized array text restored by a SpacerMap job instead. PNG/JPEG screenshots and older SVGs without metadata cannot reconstruct editable arrays. CRISPRCasFinder JSON is not an array-figure project: convert it through CRISPRPrep and SpacerMap first.

When a supported SpacerMap SVG is loaded, Preserve original SpacerMap style (colors and unique-spacer triangles) is initially checked. The same choice is available under Layout after composing.

To resume editing, select Open saved project and load the JSON produced by Save project. A supported ArrayPhyloViz SVG can also restore embedded project data when imported through the array upload control.

docs.title: Match arrays to tree leaves
docs.text:
Matching uses original Newick names, not row order or edited display labels.

Rule Example / behavior Exact names (default) strain_A matches leaf strain_A. Also strip _CRISPRn / _arrayn strain_A_CRISPR1 or strain_A_array2 can match strain_A. This is a specific suffix rule, not arbitrary substring matching. Ignore case and outer spaces Normalizes case and surrounding spaces; ambiguous normalized matches remain unassigned.

In Review and edit mapping, inspect each array's selected Tree leaf and Status. Choose the correct leaf manually when necessary. Search can narrow the mapping table. After changing the rule, Reapply name matching recomputes assignments, so recheck manual choices. Assign by leaf separately matches the part before the first underscore to an exact original leaf name: 702_NZ_JOLF01000035_1 maps to 702. It recomputes all assignments and leaves nonmatches unassigned; use Undo if needed. It cannot recover a leaf such as strain_A from strain_A_CRISPR1, because the first-underscore prefix is only strain. Use the suffix rule or manual selection in that case. Export the final correspondence with Export mapping TSV.

Several arrays can map to one strain; they form a group centered beside its leaf. Unassigned arrays remain in the project but are not drawn. Leaves with no mapped arrays remain visible. Neither an unassigned array nor an empty leaf proves biological absence: first check identifiers and mapping.

CRISPRPhylo names leaves from strain Folder; SpacerMap CSV labels combine Folder_Seq_Name when Folder is nonempty. Use Assign by leaf only when the prefix before the first underscore is the full strain name. For names containing underscores, consult the processed CSV and assign leaves manually or use a matching rule appropriate to your actual names.

docs.title: Merge or reorder arrays belonging to one leaf
docs.text:
After checking assignments, open Layout → Merge arrays by leaf:

  1. Select Merge all by leaf to place every multi-array leaf's arrays into one display row, keeping their current display order.
  2. For individual control, choose a Leaf and toggle Merge into one row.
  3. Use ↑ / ↓ to change left-to-right order when merged, or top-to-bottom order when separate.
  4. Use Undo to revert a change, or uncheck Merge into one row to separate that leaf's arrays again. Save the edited project or select Save changes.

Merging is a display operation. It retains every spacer copy and each original array in the project; it does not establish genomic adjacency, reconstruct one biological array or remove repeated IDs. Keep the mapping TSV and original processed CSV to document the underlying arrays.

docs.title: Read the combined figure
docs.text:
Read each tree leaf together with its mapped array row or rows. Matching spacer IDs show shared types in the supplied numbering scheme. Numbered TXT from unrelated runs may reuse an ID for different sequences; prepare all arrays together in SpacerMap before combining them.

The tree depicts the relationships already present in the input Newick. Arrays display spacer type and order, not base-pair distances. Shared-spacer links help follow matching IDs; they are not evidence of transfer direction. Colors and row highlights are visual annotations you control, not automatically inferred biological categories.

Use branch lengths is off by default. Enable it when you want proportional horizontal tree distances. Scaling is used only if every edge has a nonnegative length and at least one is positive; check the note below the canvas for Branch-length scale or Topology scale. Turning it off changes the drawing, not the underlying tree.

docs.title: Adjust layout and inspect details
docs.text:
Drag empty canvas space to pan. Use + / −, Ctrl/Command plus wheel, or Fit to navigate. Find locates a leaf; Expand workspace enlarges the editing area. Screen zoom does not control export resolution.

Layout control Practical use Tree layout Choose rectangular or slanted branches without changing relationships. Array alignment Right/left aligns array ends; Justify (both ends) uses SpacerMap's repeated-spacer column assignment, preserves order and expands the canvas if needed. It falls back to right alignment when no ID is repeated. Source positions uses imported positions when available. Tree width / Label space / Array width Increase the relevant region if branches, long labels or spacers are crowded. Row spacing / Label size / Branch weight Balance readability with figure size. Internal node labels / support Show labels already present in Newick; their meaning comes from the source analysis. Preserve SpacerMap style Available for imported style metadata. Retains the source palette and spacer appearance; spacer ID labels are hidden and their checkbox disabled while this is enabled. Turn it off to show IDs using the editor's style. Spacer IDs / Row guides / Export spacer legend / Shared-spacer links Include the visual aids needed by the reader. Shared-spacer links are on for new projects; saved projects retain their own setting. Shared-spacer link width Adjust line width from 0.2–8 px; enabled when shared-spacer links are shown. Filename name Set the figure's export name.

docs.title: Annotate a selection
docs.text:
1. Select a branch or node label and open Selection.
  2. Set Display label, branch/clade color, label color or clade row highlight.
  3. Select Apply annotation. Use Clear annotation to remove that styling.
  4. Use Rotate children to swap their display order, or Collapse clade to simplify a dense region. Expand all restores folded clades.

Display labels do not change matching IDs. Clade colors pass to descendants unless overridden individually. Collapsing hides detail in the view; it does not remove those descendants from the saved tree.

Select a spacer or legend item to edit fill/border colors and choose Apply to all occurrences. When an array is selected, Reverse displayed order flips its drawing only; it neither infers biological orientation nor changes source IDs. Use this deliberately and retain the project recording the edit. Undo and Redo help correct editing mistakes.

docs.title: Save an editable snapshot
docs.text:
After Commit, keep the private results link when saving succeeds. After changing mapping, annotations, layout, merging or displayed array order, select Save changes again. Each save creates a new snapshot and Job ID; old links keep their earlier state. Reopen a snapshot with Retrieve previous results or My Jobs. Snapshots expire seven days after the save task ends.

If server saving fails, the current figure remains available. Download Save project JSON or retry Save changes. A downloaded project is the durable copy for later editing. Uploading/opening a local project does not by itself save subsequent edits to an existing server link.

docs.title: Save and export
docs.text:
Control Result What to use it for Save project ArrayPhyloViz JSON with tree, original IDs, mapping, settings, labels, colors, reversed arrays, per-leaf merging/order and collapsed clades. Resume editing with Open saved project. Save before closing or refreshing. SVG Vector figure with embedded editable project data. Further figure editing and supported re-import. PNG Complete raster figure at 1×, 2× (default) or 3×, independent of screen zoom. Slides and previews. Newick Full tree in edited child order with original names and lengths. Downstream tree tools; display labels/colors are not exported as tree annotations. PDF Direct PDF download sized to the complete figure. Share a figure without the browser print dialog. Most elements remain vector; non-ASCII labels are rendered as images to preserve their appearance. Use SVG/project JSON for editable text and project state. Export mapping TSV Array-to-leaf assignments. Audit sample matching alongside the figure.

Keep the project JSON, mapping and final figure together. An image alone does not preserve a separately readable mapping report or the original sequence evidence.

docs.title: Limits and troubleshooting
docs.text:
The editor accepts one Newick up to 1 MB, 1,000 leaves, 4,000 nodes and depth 250. Array text is limited to 4 MB, with up to 1,500 arrays, 2,000 spacers per array and 20,000 total spacer instances. PNG export is limited to 32 million pixels and 16,000 pixels on either side.

Symptom Action Arrays missing beside leaves Review unassigned rows and original names; map them manually. Spacer ID checkbox is disabled Turn off Preserve SpacerMap style if you want the editor to draw ID labels. Assign by leaf loses mappings It uses only the prefix before the first underscore. Undo and use suffix matching or manual selection for strain names containing underscores. Labels overlap Increase label space or row spacing, or shorten display labels. Recoloring changes several rows Expected: spacer color applies to all occurrences of that ID. Branch lengths not reflected Enable Use branch lengths and check the layout note and input lengths. PNG too large Reduce scale or export SVG. PDF export fails Retry after refreshing the page and restoring your saved project; use SVG if PDF support could not load. Old SVG cannot be imported Use numbered TXT plus Newick, or a saved project JSON.

docs.title: SeqFetcher
docs.text: Use SeqFetcher (/ncbi-fetcher) to download nucleotide or protein records from NCBI by sequence accession, assembly accession or sequence UID. FASTA and metadata let you verify what was retrieved before continuing.

docs.title: Prepare identifiers
docs.text:
Paste IDs or upload UTF-8 .txt, .csv or .tsv containing IDs only, without a header. Separate IDs with newlines, commas, spaces or semicolons. Duplicate input IDs are removed.

NC_012920.1
NM_000546.6
NM_001126112.3

These are nucleotide retrieval examples, not a bacterial CRISPR dataset. Use sequence records corresponding to your study samples. A version suffix such as .1 identifies the requested record version.

Select Nucleotide for DNA/RNA or Protein for amino-acid records such as NP_000537.3. Numeric UIDs must belong to that database. For whole-genome assemblies, select Nucleotide and supply a GCA_ or GCF_ accession, for example GCF_000339015.1. Assembly IDs are not accepted in Protein mode. Gene, Taxonomy, BioProject and SRA IDs are not supported inputs.

docs.title: Retrieve sequences
docs.text:
1. Select the paste or upload input tab and enter IDs.
  2. Check the unique-ID count and any validation message.
  3. Select the database; keep nucleotide and protein requests in separate runs.
  4. Choose 5 · standard under IDs per request, or 1 · large sequences for large genomes. If the list contains an assembly accession, requests automatically use batch size 1.
  5. Select Commit and follow result statuses.
  6. Check organism, description and length against your sample list.

Stop after this batch requests cancellation; the active batch may finish and later IDs remain pending. Resume pending submits pending IDs as a new job. Retry failed submits all failed IDs as a new job, independently of row selection. The displayed result is replaced by the new job result; earlier successes remain accessible through the previous private link. Save that link before retrying or starting another run.

docs.title: Read results
docs.text:
Use the row statuses to follow retrieval. The downloaded run report records requested, succeeded, failed and pending counts; selected records can resolve to fewer distinct accessions.

Item Meaning Requested Unique input IDs in this run. Retrieved Input IDs resolved successfully. Failed IDs that could not be retrieved; inspect the error. Pending IDs not completed, for example after stopping or a service interruption. Unique sequences Distinct retrieved accessions. Different IDs can resolve to one accession, so this can be lower than the retrieved-record count. This is not similarity clustering. Length Nucleotide or amino-acid residues, depending on the database.

Search by ID, accession, organism or description, and use the status filter to locate unresolved records. A preview shows the FASTA header and first 2,000 characters; downloads contain the full sequence. For sequence-accession rows, View on NCBI opens the source record. For an assembly, use its GCA_/GCF_ accession to locate the corresponding NCBI assembly record.

Successful retrieval does not establish that the record is the intended strain, a complete genome or suitable CRISPR input. Verify metadata before analysis.

docs.title: Read an assembly result
docs.text:
An assembly appears as one accession row, but its FASTA can contain many chromosome/contig records. The reported length is the sum of their lengths. The downloader preserves separate FASTA headers and does not join contigs into one artificial sequence. Thus a count of one exported assembly is not necessarily one FASTA record.

The preview still shows only the first 2,000 characters; use the full FASTA download to inspect every contig. Check the assembly accession/version and metadata. An assembly package must match the requested version and its reported total length; incomplete or inconsistent downloads are reported as failures.

docs.title: Select and download
docs.text:
Retrieved rows are selected automatically. Row checkboxes change the export selection. The header checkbox affects visible retrieved rows only; previously selected hidden rows can remain selected. Check the selected-record count before export. Searching alone does not limit downloads to visible rows.

Download Contents / use FASTA Full sequences for selected records, deduplicated by accession, in one file. Metadata TSV Selected input IDs, accessions, organism, description, length and source metadata. Reconcile it with your sample list. Download ZIP Combined and individual FASTA, metadata TSV/JSON, run report, and failed/pending ID lists. Download failed IDs Unresolved IDs to check or retry later. Preview Download Complete FASTA for that accession, including all component contigs for an assembly.

Copy the private results link after submission. Retrieval continues on the server, and results can be restored through My Jobs for seven days after the task ends. Download FASTA/ZIP for longer storage. For several bacterial strains, preserve separate sample identities when continuing to CRISPRPrep; CRISPRPrep treats each uploaded FASTA file as one sample. Use individual FASTA files from the ZIP for distinct strains, or use its NCBI accession route, which groups retrieved contigs by requested ID. Protein FASTA cannot be used for genome CRISPR detection.

docs.title: Limits and recovery
docs.text:
A job accepts up to 500 unique IDs and 16,000 characters of submitted ID text; ID files are limited to 1 MB. Each request contains at most 5 IDs, or 1 when assemblies are included, and returns at most 8 million residues. The saved FASTA-text budget is 25 million characters per job, including headers and line breaks. Batch size 1 does not remove the per-response limit. Assembly packages also have a 64 MiB download/unpacked-size limit.

Symptom Action Record not found Check accession spelling/version and database. WGS master has no sequence Retrieve component records or assembly FASTA. Batch exceeds residue limit Set batch size to 1 and retry; a single record over the limit needs another retrieval workflow. Temporary NCBI failure Save the previous result link and successful outputs; retry failed/pending IDs as a new job after recovery. Download disabled Wait for retrieval to stop and select a retrieved record.

docs.title: SpacerTarget
docs.text: Use SpacerTarget (/spacer-target) to search original CRISPR spacer sequences against NCBI core_nt and inspect candidate matches in a table and strain–target network. It helps identify sequence associations worth investigating. The search does not evaluate PAMs or experimentally validate targets, infection relationships or host range.

docs.title: Prepare spacer sequences and sample identities
docs.text: Each spacer must contain 15–100 A/C/G/T bases. Resolve ambiguous bases before searching. Supply spacer sequences, not whole genomes or SpacerMap numbers. Use pasted FASTA/table text (up to 2 MB) or upload files (up to 100 files / 100 MB combined); do not combine pasted text with uploads. Additional file selections and drops append to the current upload list; check it before searching.

docs.title: FASTA
docs.text:
Use >strain|array|spacer so matches retain their strain and array assignments:

>strain_A|CRISPR1|spacer_1
CGCCAGGGTTTTCCCAGTCACGACGTTGTAAA
>strain_B|CRISPR2|spacer_1
CGCCAGGGTTTTCCCAGTCACGACGTTGTAAA

This illustrative input has two occurrences but one distinct query sequence. A match is linked back to both strains. It does not guarantee a particular NCBI result.

An alternative header is >spacer_1 strain=strain_A array=CRISPR1 source=NC_000000.1. Replace the placeholder with the real source accession if known. Source metadata enables source-record matching checks.

docs.title: CSV/TSV
docs.text:
A header is required. sequence or Spacer_Sequence supplies the original sequence. Add sample and array fields to make the network useful:

strain_id,array_id,spacer_id,sequence,source_accession
strain_A,CRISPR1,spacer_1,CGCCAGGGTTTTCCCAGTCACGACGTTGTAAA,
strain_B,CRISPR2,spacer_1,CGCCAGGGTTTTCCCAGTCACGACGTTGTAAA,

CRISPRPrep CSV is accepted: Folder becomes strain ID, Seq_Name becomes array ID and Spacer_Sequence supplies the sequence. The search uses original sequences and searches both DNA strands. It does not require replacing negative-array spacers with their reverse complements.

docs.title: CRISPRCasFinder JSON
docs.text:
Each uploaded JSON is treated as one sample. All spacer regions are included, including low/missing evidence and unknown orientation. This differs from direct JSON import in SpacerMap. Use CRISPRPrep first when you need controlled evidence/count filtering, and use CSV to specify sample grouping explicitly.

Records without strain information remain searchable and appear in the table as unassigned, but are excluded from the strain network. Identical sequences share a search while retaining all occurrences. Similar sequences and reverse complements are not collapsed into the same query.

docs.title: Start a search
docs.text:
1. Open SpacerTarget and choose Paste spacers or Upload files. Load example provides trial input.
  2. Check the input and select Maximum targets per spacer: 20, 50 · standard (default), or 100.
  3. Select Search and wait for a Job ID.
  4. Select Copy results link and save it. Paste the link or full ID under Retrieve previous results or in My Jobs to return. The current page does not offer email notification or a cache-selection control.

Spacers are sent to NCBI for the search. New submissions create new searches; there is no user-selectable cached-result reuse in the current workflow. Saved task results expire seven days after the task ends. Archive downloads and original sequences for long-term use. A higher target limit may return more candidates, but no setting guarantees an exhaustive search of phages, plasmids or all database matches.

docs.title: Follow progress and recover
docs.text:
Progress follows Queued → Search → Annotate → Complete, with Waiting for resources when local capacity is temporarily unavailable. A task is split into batches of at most 10 distinct spacers and 1,000 bases. Local queue waiting and remote NCBI searching are different stages. Searching finds sequence matches; annotation retrieves target metadata. Read Details for batch warnings and unresolved steps. The activity display is not an estimated time remaining. Once a batch has a remote request ID, its NCBI request link opens the NCBI request page; this remote ID is different from the CRISPREvo Job ID. Slow remote searching does not by itself mean no hits.

Closing the tab does not cancel a submitted task. Use the saved results link or ID to return. Refresh checks the current state; it does not start another search. Cancel stops future work while retaining successful results; a request already sent to NCBI may still run. After a task ends, the input is deleted and in-place retry is unavailable. Keep any successful results, then resubmit the needed original spacer sequences as a new task.

A partial, failed or cancelled task can still contain successful matches. Do not interpret those as a completed search of all input spacers. Anyone with the results link can access the task, so share it only with intended collaborators. The results link and local history do not extend the seven-day retention period.

docs.title: Choose match-quality filters
docs.text:
Results initially use Strict. Changing filters reuses retrieved evidence and does not launch another BLAST search.

Preset Keeps Strict Full spacer coverage, at most 2 mismatches, no gaps. Exact Full coverage, no mismatches and no gaps. Explore Custom minimum identity (default 90%), minimum coverage (90%) and maximum mismatches (100). Gapped alignments may pass.

Filter further by Target type, Strain and search text. Sort changes ordering only. Exclude source-accession matches removes hits matching the supplied source_accession, ignoring version suffixes. Without a source accession, a row cannot be identified as a source-record match. This control does not detect every self-target or automatically exclude all CRISPR array regions.

Use Reset filters to clear table filters and any node/edge focus. Network Show checkboxes only hide target categories in the graph; they do not apply the table's Target type filter or restrict TSV exports.

docs.title: Read the match table
docs.text:
One row is one spacer occurrence matched to one target site. Repeated sequences in different strains, different sites on one accession, and different accessions can produce multiple rows. Row count is not a count of distinct spacer sequences or unique targets.

Field Interpretation Strain / spacer Original sample/array/spacer assignment. Target sequence Matched accession and description. Open its source record to check context. Type Virus/phage, plasmid, chromosome or unknown, inferred from available source annotations and taxonomy. Unknown can reflect missing or incomplete annotation. Identity Identical nucleotide columns divided by alignment length, including gap columns in the denominator. Coverage Aligned non-gap query bases as a percentage of the spacer's full length. 100% identity with partial coverage is not a full-length exact match. Mismatch / gap Different nucleotide positions and gap-containing alignment columns, reported separately. Target coordinates 1-based inclusive start/end on the target record; strand is relative to the submitted query. A minus-strand hit is not an error. E-value BLAST's expectation statistic. Use it alongside coverage, mismatches and alignment context; it is not a probability that the target is biologically valid. Alignment Opens aligned query and target sequences, match markers and an NCBI link for close inspection.

For example, a 32-base spacer aligned over all 32 bases with one mismatch and no gaps has 100% coverage and 96.875% identity. It passes Strict but not Exact. Separate local alignments are not stitched together to claim full-length coverage.

A chromosome hit can include the source array or other genomic similarity. A virus/phage label does not establish host range. No displayed rows can mean no returned candidates, all candidates filtered out, or unfinished/failed queries. First check task completion, then Explore, Reset filters and All candidates TSV before interpreting absence.

docs.title: Read the strain–target network
docs.text:
Nodes represent strains and target accessions. Each edge joins one strain to one target and is weighted by the number of different supporting spacer sequences under the current table filters. Repeated copies or multiple alignments of one sequence do not increase that weight. A thicker line means more distinct spacer support, not stronger experimentally measured interaction.

Click a node to focus the table on that strain or target; click an edge to focus both. Drag nodes to arrange, drag background to pan, use zoom or Fit network, and choose Clustered, Force directed or Circle layout. Layout proximity and connected groups are visual summaries, not phylogenetic distances.

The graph displays up to 200 nodes and reports hidden nodes/edges. Table and TSV exports retain all filtered matches. Unassigned spacers are omitted from the graph. An empty or smaller graph does not mean the table lost those results.

docs.title: Download and preserve evidence
docs.text:
Download What it contains Export filtered TSV All rows passing current table filters and node/edge focus, across every table page. All candidates TSV All returned candidate alignments, without Strict or current table filtering. This is not every possible match in the database. Search report JSON containing occurrence/query IDs, retained batch match evidence, annotation status, timestamps and errors. Terminal reports omit full original query sequences, search parameters and raw BLAST responses. Network PNG / SVG Current network view/layout. Preserve TSV/report as the underlying evidence.

Keep original input sequences and separately record database, hit limit and filter thresholds. Save the search report, all-candidate TSV and a filtered TSV for the evidence used in your analysis. In terminal results, the exported sequence field can be blank because full input sequences were deleted; occurrence/query identifiers and alignment strings remain. Do not reconstruct a complete spacer from a partial alignment. Search text for a full original sequence may no longer work after completion; use strain/spacer IDs or target accessions instead.

docs.title: Limits and troubleshooting
docs.text:
A task accepts up to 100 distinct spacers, 10,000 occurrences, 100 uploaded files / 100 MB combined, or 2 MB pasted input. The sequence/occurrence limits still apply to large uploaded JSON files. Each spacer is 15–100 A/C/G/T bases. Both strands are searched. A submitted search batch exceeding 24 hours is marked failed; inspect task details and resubmit the needed original input in a new task.

Symptom Action Search disabled Check service status with Refresh status; the search service must be available. Invalid spacer Supply original sequence, check length, and resolve N or other ambiguous symbols. No strain network Add strain_id or three-part FASTA headers; confirm that retained matches exist. Unknown target type Inspect annotation status; unknown is not proof that the target is nonviral/nonplasmid. Strict gives no rows Check completion, inspect all candidates, then use Explore to examine partial/lower-quality matches. Target limit reached Treat candidate lists as truncated; consider a fresh search with a higher supported limit.

docs.title: SpacerMap
docs.text: Use SpacerMap (/spacer-map) to compare spacer order and sharing across CRISPR arrays. It produces an array diagram, per-spacer array counts, a presence/absence chart and, when clustering is enabled, an array network. Genome FASTA must first go through CRISPRPrep.

docs.title: Prepare your input
docs.text:
Choose one input source per run. Leave the paste box empty when uploading.

Input How to prepare it Numbered arrays Paste one named array per line, or upload TXT/TSV. Each number identifies a spacer type. Spacer sequences in a table Paste or upload Processed CSV from CRISPRPrep, retaining its header; each row is one spacer. CRISPRPrep can also transfer it directly. CRISPRCasFinder JSON Upload one JSON. Direct import keeps evidence levels 3–4 and applies fixed direction/N filters. Use CRISPRPrep first to control filtering. Spacer FASTA Upload one FASTA containing one array, with one record per spacer. The filename becomes the array name. This is not whole-genome input. Direction folders Select a folder with spacer FASTA files under pos/forward or neg/reverse. Each file is one array. Arrays written as DNA sequences Upload TXT/TSV with one named array per line. Use upload for sequence-to-number conversion; pasted array-format text is treated as labels, while a recognized CSV header triggers CSV conversion.

Paste this three-array example. The page's Load example supplies a separate, alignment-dependent example:

strain_A_CRISPR1    1,2,3,6,7,9
strain_B_CRISPR1    1,2,4,6,8,9
strain_C_CRISPR1    10,2,4,6,8

Use a tab between each name and list. Keep array names unique. For CSV, SpacerMap combines nonempty Folder and Seq_Name as Folder_Seq_Name; without Folder it uses Seq_Name alone. For example, Folder 702 and Seq_Name NZ_JOLF01000035_1 produce 702_NZ_JOLF01000035_1. Different samples can reuse an array name if their combined labels differ. Avoid collisions caused by underscores in custom field values, and use one consistent orientation per combined label.

docs.title: Choose alignment and clustering
docs.text:
Alignment What changes When it helps Right (default) Last spacers line up at the right edge. Compare ends of consistently oriented arrays. Left First spacers line up at the left edge. Compare starting blocks. Justify Shared spacers guide horizontal spacing while preserving order. Follow shared internal blocks across arrays of different lengths.

Alignment is a drawing choice. Left/right does not determine the biological leader or trailer end. Establish orientation from your source data before assigning acquisition direction. Justified gaps are visual spacing, not measured genomic gaps or proof of deletion.

Clustering Exact grouping rule Interpretation No clustering Keeps input row order. Useful when samples already have a meaningful order. Shared spacer (default) Links pairs sharing at least two distinct IDs; connected arrays form a group. Two arrays can join through a third without sharing two IDs directly. Ancestral spacer Groups arrays with the same rightmost spacer ID. A terminal-spacer grouping heuristic; it does not reconstruct an ancestor or establish which spacer is oldest.

Clustering reorders rows, never spacer order within an already normalized array. After a completed run, changing alignment or clustering automatically updates the current preview using its normalized arrays. These preview-only changes do not overwrite the saved job. To preserve them, download the current SVG or select Commit and save the new job link. On a fresh page the defaults are Right / Shared spacer; select No clustering explicitly when input row order matters.

docs.title: Run and read the diagram
docs.text:
1. Paste the example or upload your input.
  2. Select alignment and clustering; Right and No clustering are a useful first view.
  3. Select Commit and wait for the preview.
  4. Check array names, spacer IDs and the displayed alignment/clustering. Use Spacer occurrence below for per-ID counts.
  5. With clustering enabled, select Show cluster network to inspect pairwise connections.

Each row is an array; each symbol is one spacer occurrence. IDs identify types within this dataset. Shared types use consistent colors. Types found in only one array are drawn as triangles, including every repeated copy within that array. A triangle means array-specific, not necessarily a spacer seen only once. Use IDs as the primary reference when colors look similar.

Links between neighboring rows connect matching spacer IDs. A break in links does not by itself identify a biological gain or loss. Check IDs, order and orientation together.

Distinct spacer labels are different IDs, not the total number of symbols. Shared labels occur in at least two arrays. Use the occurrence table below to inspect how many arrays contain each ID. The example above has 3 arrays, 9 distinct labels and 6 shared labels, with 17 total occurrences. IDs 3, 7 and 10 are array-specific.

In the cluster network, nodes are arrays. A line indicates that the pair meets the selected grouping rule. Network proximity is a layout aid, not evolutionary distance. The network is unavailable with No clustering. Select a node to see its array, cluster and connection count; select an edge to see the pair and shared-ID count. Drag nodes to rearrange them or drag the background to pan. Use Ctrl + scroll (Command + scroll on Mac), zoom buttons or Fit network to navigate. Choose Force-directed, Circle or Grid, and use Reset layout to recalculate the layout. Its Download SVG and Download PNG buttons export the network separately from the array map.

docs.title: Navigate and recover the preview
docs.text:
Drag to pan and use Ctrl + scroll (Command + scroll on Mac) to zoom. Scrolling without a modifier scrolls the page. The + / − and Fit controls adjust the preview; with the preview focused, 0 fits the diagram and arrow keys pan. These changes do not crop or resize exported figures.

Rendering creates a saved job. Copy its private results link to restore SVG, normalized array text, any sequence-to-ID mapping, occurrence statistics, alignment, clustering and seed through My Jobs for seven days after the task ends. Keep your original data, array-map SVG and sequence mapping for reruns. Changing the seed triggers another render; save the link for the version you intend to retain. Recovery fills the input box with normalized array text, not the original sequence upload. Copy that text if you need reusable array-per-line TXT. Recommitting it preserves IDs and order but cannot regenerate a sequence mapping; keep the original mapping download or reselect original sequence input when needed.

docs.title: Count how widely each spacer occurs
docs.text:
Use Spacer occurrence to compare the number of arrays containing each spacer ID. This panel uses the normalized arrays from the last completed run, including sequence-to-ID conversion when applicable. It is available with No clustering as well as either clustering mode.

  1. Submit your input with Commit and wait for the array diagram.
  2. Select Spacer statistics in the page navigation, or scroll to Spacer occurrence.
  3. Expand View spacer counts (first 100; CSV includes all) to read the counts without drawing a chart.
  4. Select Show occurrence chart to display the bar chart and presence/absence matrix. Select Hide occurrence chart to collapse it again. Scroll inside the preview when the figure is wider or taller than the visible area.
  5. Use the Format, DPI and download controls at the bottom of this panel for statistics exports. These controls are separate from the array-map export controls.

docs.title: What the counts mean
docs.text:
Number of arrays counts each array once for each spacer ID, even if that ID occurs several times in that array. It is neither total spacer copies nor the number of strains. If one strain contributes several arrays, each array is counted separately. Counts reflect the arrays retained in this run, not every array originally detected before filtering.

For the three-array example above, the expected counts are:

Spacer IDs Number of arrays Interpretation 2, 6 3 Present in every input array. 1, 9, 4, 8 2 Shared by two input arrays. 3, 7, 10 1 Restricted to one input array.

The chart sorts IDs by decreasing count. Ties follow first appearance in the normalized input, so it is not a numeric-ID sort. For this example the columns are 2, 6, 1, 9, 4, 8, 3, 7, 10. Matrix rows retain input array order; clustering can reorder the main array diagram without changing these statistics.

This figure uses the short array names in the quick-start input. The counts are identical to the example above. Download its statistics CSV to compare with your export.

In the upper panel, bar height and the number above each bar give Number of arrays. In the lower matrix, each column is that same spacer ID and each row is an array: a filled circle means present; a hollow circle means absent from that array's retained input. The matrix does not show copy number, spacer order or genomic position. Absence from the input is not, by itself, evidence of a biological loss.

For example, array_A: 1,1,2 and array_B: 2,3 contain five spacer copies, but the array counts for IDs 1, 2 and 3 are 1, 2 and 1. Repeated ID 1 does not increase its bar to 2. These statistics use SpacerMap IDs, so similarity-grouped sequences can contribute to the same count; they do not establish exact nucleotide identity.

Colors connect each bar with its matrix column. They use a separate deterministic palette of 50 distinct colors, which can still look similar; read the ID labels rather than matching colors between panels. Changing the map's Seed does not change occurrence counts or this chart's palette. Changing alignment or clustering also leaves counts unchanged for the same normalized input.

docs.title: Export the statistics
docs.text:
Control / format Output and scope Download statistics CSV SpacerMap-occurrence.csv, with columns Spacer ID and Number of arrays. Includes every distinct spacer ID, even when the on-page table shows only the first 100 or charting is unavailable. SVG, PDF, EPS The complete bar chart and presence/absence matrix in one vector figure. DPI is disabled for these formats. PNG, JPG, TIFF, WEBP The same complete figure as a raster image. Set a whole-number DPI from 36 to 2,400; the default is 300.

Choose a format and select Download SVG, Download PDF, or the corresponding download button. Image files are named SpacerMap-occurrence.<format>. You can download a figure without first opening its preview. CSV contains counts, not the matrix or original sequences, so keep the numbered input with it.

Charts require 1–50 distinct spacer IDs and include all of them. If there are more than 50, both chart preview and chart export are disabled; the tool does not silently show a top-50 subset. The statistics CSV still includes every ID. To make a smaller chart, select a meaningful subset, submit it as a new run and clearly identify that subset when reporting its counts. Reuse numbered input if you need consistent IDs across subsets.

Raster statistics exports are limited to 40 million pixels. If export exceeds this limit, lower DPI or use SVG/PDF. SVG/PDF/EPS still require no more than 50 distinct IDs. An occurrence SVG is a statistics figure and cannot replace the metadata-bearing array-map SVG used in ArrayPhyloViz.

Statistics can be recovered with saved results when the normalized array data is available. If an older result reports that statistics are unavailable, resubmit the original or saved numbered input. Editing the input box alone does not update a completed run's counts; select Commit again.

docs.title: Understand automatic spacer numbering
docs.text:
For sequence inputs, sequences with pairwise global-alignment identity of at least 0.84 are connected, and each connected group receives an ID. Similar sequences can share an ID without being identical; transitive groups can include members below 0.84 identity to one another. Numbering depends on the dataset and ordering. ID 1 in two independent runs is not a universal spacer identity.

CSV/JSON and direction-folder inputs use orientation information during conversion. CSV rows keep their supplied order for both strands: CRISPRPrep has already reversed negative-array row order, and SpacerMap does not reverse it again. Negative CSV rows use Reverse_Complement_Sequence, or compute it when missing. CSV rows with ND are skipped. Direction-folder conversion applies its own negative-array ordering rule, so inspect the result when changing input routes. Already numbered input is drawn in supplied order. Numeric FASTA headers are used directly as IDs.

Reuse the same normalized array text or metadata-bearing array-map SVG when comparing figures. Download numbered file is an ID–sequence lookup, not array input. For sequence-level searches, retain original sequences and use SpacerTarget; numeric IDs cannot be searched.

docs.title: Export and continue
docs.text:
For the array diagram, in Customize export, set Seed, Format and, for raster output, DPI. Seed defaults to 2 and changes colors, not IDs or clustering. Wait for the preview update before downloading. Preserve the same dataset, order and seed to reproduce the palette.

Output Use it for SVG Scalable figures and importing array metadata into ArrayPhyloViz. PNG Slides or image previews. JPG/JPEG, TIF/TIFF, WEBP Workflows requiring these formats. Raster DPI defaults to 300; allowed range is 36–2,400. Download numbered file Tab-separated .txt with Spacer_ID and Spacer_Sequence, one row per distinct ID–sequence pair. Similarity-grouped variants can share an ID. Negative CSV spacers use the reverse complement used for numbering. No array names, membership or order are included. Number-only input has no sequence mapping.

To combine arrays with a tree, open ArrayPhyloViz, upload a newly exported array-map SVG and add a Newick tree. SVG carries array membership, ordered IDs, colors and source positions. An existing one-array-per-line TXT also works, but the ID–sequence mapping from Download numbered file does not. To save normalized array TXT, retrieve the job and copy the restored input text; the saved result report also includes export_text.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check No usable JSON arrays Direct import excludes low evidence, unresolved ND and organisms with N-containing spacers. Use CRISPRPrep to see exclusion reasons. Two samples appear as one row Inspect combined Folder_Seq_Name labels; without Folder, Seq_Name alone must be unique. Unexpected shared IDs Numbering groups similar sequences; inspect original sequences for exact identity. No cluster network Select a clustering mode and wait for the preview update. Isolated nodes are valid when no pair meets the rule. Occurrence chart is disabled Check the distinct-ID count: charts require 1–50 IDs. Download the statistics CSV for larger datasets. A count is lower than the number of copies Each array contributes at most one count per ID, even with repeated spacers. Statistics panel could not load Reload the page and retrieve the saved job. The array input and map can still work independently. ID–sequence download fails as array input Use the array-map SVG in ArrayPhyloViz or restore/copy normalized array text; the mapping file has no array membership. IDs/colors differ between analyses Reuse the same normalized array input and seed; IDs are not global across datasets.
